title: V. By Ilusha’s Bedside
paragraphs: The room occupied by the family of the retired captain Snegiryov is already familiar to the reader. It was close and crowded just then with a number of visitors. Several boys were sitting with Ilusha, and though all of them, like Smurov, would have denied that it was Alyosha who'd brought them there and reconciled them with Ilusha, that was in fact the truth. All the skill he'd used had been to bring them, one by one, to see Ilusha, without any "soppy sentimentality," making it look casual and unplanned. It was a great comfort to Ilusha in his suffering. He was deeply touched by the almost tender affection and sympathy these boys — his former enemies — showed him. Krassotkin was the only one missing, and his absence weighed heavily on Ilusha's heart. Perhaps the bitterest of all his bitter memories was stabbing Krassotkin, who had been his one friend and protector. Clever little Smurov, the first to make peace with Ilusha, thought that was the reason. But when Smurov hinted to Krassotkin that Alyosha wanted to come see him about something, Krassotkin cut him off, telling Smurov to tell "Karamazov" right away that he knew perfectly well what to do, that he wanted no one's advice, and that if he went to see Ilusha he'd choose his own time, since he had "his own reasons."

That was a fortnight before this Sunday. That was why Alyosha hadn't gone to see him, as he'd meant to. But though he waited, he sent Smurov to him twice more. Both times Krassotkin met him with a curt, impatient refusal, sending word back to Alyosha not to bother him anymore, and that if he came himself, he, Krassotkin, wouldn't go to Ilusha's at all. Right up until the last day, Smurov had no idea Kolya meant to go to Ilusha's that morning, and only the evening before, as he parted from Smurov, Kolya abruptly told him to wait at home for him the next morning, since he'd go with him to the Snegiryovs' — but warned him not to breathe a word that he was coming, since he wanted to drop in casually. Smurov obeyed. Smurov's guess that Kolya would bring back the lost dog was based on something Kolya had let slip — that "they must be asses not to find the dog, if it's alive." When Smurov, waiting for the right moment, timidly hinted at his guess about the dog, Krassotkin flew into a violent rage. "I'm not such an ass as to go hunting all over town for other people's dogs when I've got a dog of my own! And how can you imagine a dog could stay alive after swallowing a pin? Soppy sentimentality, that's all it is!"

For the last fortnight Ilusha hadn't left his little bed under the icons in the corner. He hadn't been to school since the day he met Alyosha and bit his finger. He fell ill that very same day, though for a month afterward he could sometimes still get up and walk around the room and hallway. But lately he'd grown so weak he couldn't move without his father's help. His father was terribly worried about him. He'd even given up drinking and was nearly out of his mind with fear that his boy would die. And often, especially after leading him around the room on his arm and putting him back to bed, he'd rush off to a dark corner in the hallway, lean his head against the wall, and break into fits of violent weeping, stifling his sobs so Ilusha wouldn't hear them.

Coming back into the room, he'd usually start doing something to amuse and comfort his precious boy — telling him stories, funny anecdotes, or mimicking comic people he'd happened to meet, even imitating the howls and cries of animals. But Ilusha couldn't bear watching his father clown and play the buffoon. Though the boy tried not to show how much he disliked it, he saw, with an aching heart, that his father was an object of ridicule, and he was continually haunted by the memory of the "wisp of tow" and that "terrible day."

Nina, Ilusha's gentle, crippled sister, didn't care for her father's buffoonery either (Varvara had gone off some time before to Petersburg to study at the university). But the half-witted mother found it hugely entertaining, and laughed heartily whenever her husband started capering about or performing something. It was the only way she could be amused; the rest of the time she grumbled and complained that everyone had forgotten her now, that no one treated her with respect, that she was slighted, and so on. But over the last few days she'd changed completely. She'd started staring constantly at Ilusha's bed in the corner, seeming lost in thought. She was quieter, more subdued, and, if she cried, she cried softly so as not to be heard. The captain noticed the change in her with mournful bewilderment. The boys' visits had at first only irritated her, but later their cheerful shouting and stories began to entertain her, and eventually she grew so fond of them that, if the boys had stopped coming, she'd have felt lonely without them. When the children told a story or played a game, she laughed and clapped her hands. She called some of them over and kissed them. She was especially fond of Smurov.

As for the captain, having the children in his room, coming to cheer up Ilusha, filled his heart from the start with ecstatic joy. He even hoped Ilusha would now shake off his depression, and that it would speed his recovery. Despite his fear for Ilusha, he hadn't, until lately, doubted for a moment that his boy would ultimately recover.

He greeted his young visitors with deference, waited on them hand and foot, and was ready to be their horse — even let them ride on his back — but Ilusha didn't like the game, so it was dropped. He started buying little treats for them, gingerbread and nuts, gave them tea, cut them sandwiches. It should be noted that all this time he had plenty of money. He'd taken the two hundred roubles from Katerina Ivanovna, just as Alyosha had predicted he would. And afterward Katerina Ivanovna, learning more about their circumstances and about Ilusha's illness, visited them herself, got to know the family, and managed to charm the half-witted mother. Since then she'd been generous in helping them, and the captain, terrified at the thought his boy might be dying, set aside his pride and humbly accepted her help.

All this time Doctor Herzenstube, called in by Katerina Ivanovna, came punctually every other day, but little came of his visits, and he dosed the poor invalid mercilessly. But that Sunday morning a new doctor was expected, one who'd come from Moscow with a great reputation. Katerina Ivanovna had sent for him from Moscow at considerable expense, not specifically for Ilusha, but for another purpose, of which more will be said in its place further on. But, since he'd come, she'd asked him to see Ilusha as well, and the captain had been told to expect him. He had no idea whatsoever that Kolya Krassotkin was coming, though he'd long hoped for a visit from the boy Ilusha was pining for.

At the moment Krassotkin opened the door and came into the room, the captain and all the boys were gathered around Ilusha's bed, looking at a tiny mastiff pup, only born the day before, though the captain had ordered it a week earlier to comfort and amuse Ilusha, still grieving over the lost and probably dead Zhutchka. Ilusha, who'd heard three days before that he was to be given a puppy — not just any puppy, but a pedigree mastiff, a very important point, of course — tried, out of delicacy, to pretend he was pleased. But his father and the boys couldn't help seeing that the puppy only served to remind his little heart of the poor dog he'd killed. The puppy lay beside him, feebly stirring, and he, smiling sadly, stroked it with his thin, pale, wasted hand. He clearly liked the puppy, but ... it wasn't Zhutchka; if he could have had both Zhutchka and the puppy, then he'd have been completely happy.
"Krassotkin!" one of the boys suddenly cried. He was the first to see him come in.
Krassotkin's entrance caused a general stir; the boys stepped back and lined up on either side of the bed, so he could see Ilusha clearly. The captain rushed eagerly to meet Kolya.
"Please, come in ... you're most welcome!" he said hurriedly. "Ilusha, Mr. Krassotkin has come to see you!"

But Krassotkin, shaking his hand hastily, immediately demonstrated his complete grasp of proper manners. He turned first to the captain's wife, sitting in her armchair, who was in a rather sour mood just then, grumbling that the boys were standing between her and Ilusha's bed and blocking her view of the new puppy. With the greatest courtesy he bowed to her, scraping his foot, and, turning to Nina, gave her, as the only other lady present, a similar bow. This polite behavior made an extremely favorable impression on the deranged lady.
"There, you can tell at once he's a young man who's been well brought up," she remarked aloud, throwing up her hands; "but as for our other visitors, they come piling in one on top of another."
"What do you mean, mamma, one on top of another? How's that?" the captain muttered affectionately, though with a hint of anxiety on her account.
"That's how they come riding in. They climb on each other's shoulders out in the passage and go prancing in like that, into a respectable family's home. Strange sort of visitors!"
"But who came in like that, mamma?"
"Why, that boy came riding in on that one's back, and this one on that one's."

Kolya was already at Ilusha's bedside. The sick boy went visibly pale. He raised himself in the bed and stared intently at Kolya. Kolya hadn't seen his little friend in two months, and he was stunned at the sight of him. He'd never imagined he'd see such a wasted, yellow face, such huge, feverishly glowing eyes, such thin little hands. He saw, with grieved surprise, Ilusha's quick, labored breathing and his dry lips. He stepped close, held out his hand, and, nearly overcome, said:

"Well, old man ... how are you?" But his voice failed him; he couldn't manage an easy tone; his face suddenly twitched and the corners of his mouth trembled. Ilusha smiled a pitiful little smile, still unable to say a word. Something made Kolya raise his hand and run it over Ilusha's hair.
"Never mind!" he murmured softly, to cheer him up, or maybe without even knowing why he said it. For a minute they were silent again.
"Hey, so you've got a new puppy?" Kolya said suddenly, in a thoroughly offhand voice.
"Ye—es," Ilusha answered in a long whisper, gasping for breath.

"A black nose — that means he'll be fierce, a good watchdog," Kolya observed gravely and stolidly, as though the puppy and its black nose were the only thing on his mind. But in truth he was still struggling with all his might not to burst into tears like a child, and try as he might, he couldn't quite manage it. "When he's grown, you'll have to keep him on a chain, I'm sure."
"He'll be a huge dog!" one of the boys cried.
"Of course he will," "a mastiff," "big," "like this," "big as a calf," several voices shouted.

"Big as a calf, a real calf," the captain chimed in. "I got one like that on purpose, one of the fiercest breeds, and his parents are huge and very fierce — they stand this high off the floor.... Sit down here, on Ilusha's bed, or here on the bench. You're welcome, we've been hoping to see you a long time.... You were kind enough to come with Alexey Fyodorovitch?"
Krassotkin sat on the edge of the bed, at Ilusha's feet. Though he'd perhaps prepared some easy, casual opening for the conversation on the way over, he now completely lost the thread of it.

"No ... I came with Perezvon. I've got a dog now, called Perezvon. A Slavonic name. He's out there ... if I whistle, he'll come running in. I brought a dog too," he said, suddenly addressing Ilusha. "Do you remember Zhutchka, old man?" he fired the question at him abruptly.

Ilusha's little face quivered. He looked at Kolya with an anguished expression. Alyosha, standing by the door, frowned and signaled to Kolya not to mention Zhutchka, but Kolya either didn't notice or wouldn't.
"Where ... is Zhutchka?" Ilusha asked in a broken voice.
"Oh, well, my boy, your Zhutchka's lost and gone for good!"
Ilusha said nothing, but fixed an intent gaze on Kolya once more. Alyosha, catching Kolya's eye, signaled to him again, more urgently, but Kolya looked away, pretending not to notice.

"He must have run off and died somewhere. Must have died after a meal like that," Kolya pronounced pitilessly, though he seemed a little out of breath himself. "But I've got a dog, Perezvon ... a Slavonic name.... I brought him to show you."
"I don't want him!" Ilusha said suddenly.

"No, no, you really must see him ... it'll cheer you up. I brought him on purpose.... He's the same kind of shaggy dog.... Will you let me call my dog in, madam?" he suddenly asked Madame Snegiryov, with an inexplicable excitement in his manner.
"I don't want him, I don't want him!" Ilusha cried, a mournful break in his voice. There was a reproachful light in his eyes.

"You'd better," the captain started up from the chest by the wall, where he'd just sat down, "you'd better ... another time," he muttered, but Kolya couldn't be held back. He hurriedly shouted to Smurov, "Open the door," and as soon as it opened, he blew his whistle. Perezvon dashed headlong into the room.

"Jump, Perezvon, beg! Beg!" Kolya shouted, jumping up, and the dog rose on its hind legs at Ilusha's bedside. What followed took everyone by surprise: Ilusha started, lurched violently forward, bent over Perezvon, and stared at him, faint with suspense.
"It's ... Zhutchka!" he suddenly cried, in a voice breaking with joy and anguish.
"And who did you think it was?" Krassotkin shouted with all his might, in a ringing, joyful voice, and, bending down, he seized the dog and lifted him up to Ilusha.

"Look, old man, you see — blind in one eye, left ear torn, exactly the marks you described to me. That's how I found him. I found him right away. He didn't belong to anyone!" he explained, turning quickly to the captain, to his wife, to Alyosha, and then back to Ilusha. "He'd been living in the Fedotovs' back yard. He made his home there, but they never fed him. He was a stray that had run off from the village ... I found him.... You see, old man, he couldn't have swallowed what you gave him. If he had, he'd have died, he'd have had to! So he must have spat it out, since he's alive. You didn't see him do it. But the pin pricked his tongue, that's why he squealed. He ran off squealing and you thought he'd swallowed it. He might well squeal — the skin inside a dog's mouth is so tender ... much more tender than in people!" Kolya cried impetuously, his face glowing, radiant with delight. Ilusha couldn't speak. White as a sheet, he stared open-mouthed at Kolya, his huge eyes almost starting out of his head. And if Krassotkin, who had no idea of it, had known what a devastating, even fatal effect a moment like this might have on the sick boy's health, nothing would have induced him to play such a trick on him. But Alyosha was perhaps the only person in the room who understood that. As for the captain, he behaved like a small child.
"Zhutchka! It's Zhutchka!" he cried in a voice full of bliss. "Ilusha, this is Zhutchka, your Zhutchka! Mamma, this is Zhutchka!" He was nearly weeping.
"And I never guessed!" Smurov cried regretfully. "Bravo, Krassotkin! I said he'd find the dog, and here he's found him."
"Here he's found him!" another boy echoed gleefully.
"Krassotkin's a brick!" a third voice cried.
"He's a brick, he's a brick!" the other boys cried, and started clapping.

"Wait, wait," Krassotkin did his utmost to shout over them all. "I'll tell you how it happened, that's the whole point. I found him, took him home, and hid him right away. I kept him locked up at home and didn't show him to anyone until today. Only Smurov's known for the last fortnight, but I told him this dog was called Perezvon, and he never guessed. And meanwhile I taught the dog all sorts of tricks. You should see everything he can do! I trained him so I could bring you a well-trained dog, in good condition, old man, so I could say to you, 'See, old man, what a fine dog your Zhutchka is now!' Have you got a bit of meat? He'll show you a trick that'll make you die laughing. A bit of meat, have you got any?"

The captain dashed across the passage to the landlady's, where their cooking was done. Not wanting to lose precious time, Kolya, in desperate haste, shouted to Perezvon, "Dead!" And the dog immediately turned around and lay on his back with all four paws in the air. The boys laughed. Ilusha watched with the same suffering smile, but the one most delighted by the dog's performance was "mamma." She laughed at the dog and began snapping her fingers and calling him, "Perezvon, Perezvon!"

"Nothing will make him get up, nothing!" Kolya cried triumphantly, proud of his success. "He won't budge for all the shouting in the world, but if I call him, he'll jump up in a second. Ici, Perezvon!" The dog leapt up and bounded about, whining with delight. The captain ran back with a piece of cooked beef.

"Is it hot?" Kolya asked briskly, businesslike, taking the meat. "Dogs don't like hot things. No, it's fine. Look, everyone, look, Ilusha, look, old man — why aren't you looking? He's not looking, now that I've brought him."

The new trick was to make the dog stand motionless, nose out, with a tempting bit of meat balanced right on his nose. The luckless dog had to stand without moving, meat balanced on his nose, for as long as his master chose to keep him there — sometimes as long as half an hour. But this time he kept Perezvon waiting only a moment.
"Paid for!" Kolya cried, and the meat flashed from the dog's nose straight into his mouth. The audience, of course, burst into applause and exclamations of amazement.
"Can you really have put off coming all this time simply to train the dog?" Alyosha exclaimed, an unintended note of reproach in his voice.
"Simply for that!" Kolya answered, with perfect simplicity. "I wanted to show him off in all his glory."
"Perezvon! Perezvon," Ilusha called suddenly, snapping his thin fingers and beckoning to the dog.

"What is it? Let him jump up on the bed! _Ici_, Perezvon!" Kolya slapped the bed, and Perezvon sprang up beside Ilusha. The boy threw both arms around his head, and Perezvon instantly licked his cheek. Ilusha pressed close to him, stretched out in bed, and hid his face in the dog's shaggy coat.
"Dear, dear!" the captain kept exclaiming. Kolya sat back down on the edge of the bed.
"Ilusha, I can show you another trick. I've brought you a little cannon. Remember, I told you about it before, and you said how much you'd like to see it. Well, here, I brought it for you."

And Kolya hurriedly pulled the little bronze cannon out of his satchel. He hurried because he was happy himself. Another time he'd have waited for the excitement over Perezvon to die down first, but now he pressed ahead, heedless of any such consideration. "You're all happy now," he felt, "so here's something to make you happier still!" He was utterly delighted himself.

"I've been coveting this thing for a long while — it's for you, old man, it's for you. It belonged to Morozov, it was no use to him, he had it from his brother. I traded him a book from father's bookcase for it — _A Kinsman of Mahomet, or Salutary Folly_, a scandalous book published in Moscow a hundred years ago, before there was any censorship. And Morozov has a taste for that sort of thing. He was grateful to me for it, too...."

Kolya held the cannon in his hand so everyone could see and admire it. Ilusha raised himself, and, still with his right arm around the dog, gazed at the toy in delight. The excitement grew even greater when Kolya announced he had gunpowder too, and that it could be fired off right there "if it won't alarm the ladies." "Mamma" immediately asked to look at the toy up close, and her request was granted. She was thoroughly pleased with the little bronze cannon on wheels, and began rolling it back and forth on her lap. She readily gave permission for the cannon to be fired, without the slightest idea what she was agreeing to. Kolya showed the powder and the shot. The captain, being a military man, took charge of loading it, putting in a tiny amount of powder. He asked that the shot be saved for another time. The cannon was set on the floor, aimed at an empty part of the room, three grains of powder were pushed into the touch-hole, and a match was struck. A magnificent bang followed. Mamma was startled, but immediately laughed with delight. The boys stared in speechless triumph. But the captain, watching Ilusha, was more delighted than any of them. Kolya picked up the cannon and at once presented it to Ilusha, along with the powder and shot.
"I got it for you, for you! I've been saving it for you a long time," he repeated once more, delighted.
"Oh, give it to me! No, give me the cannon!" mamma began begging like a little child. Her face showed a pitiful fear that she wouldn't get it. Kolya was thrown off. The captain fidgeted uneasily.

"Mamma, mamma," he ran to her, "the cannon's yours, of course, but let Ilusha have it, since it's a present to him — but it's just as much yours. Ilusha will always let you play with it; it'll belong to both of you, both of you."
"No, I don't want it to belong to both of us, I want it to be mine, entirely, not Ilusha's," mamma insisted, on the point of tears.

"Take it, mother, here, keep it!" Ilusha cried. "Krassotkin, may I give it to my mother?" he turned to Krassotkin with a pleading face, as though afraid he might be offended at his giving the present away to someone else.
"Of course you may," Krassotkin agreed warmly, and, taking the cannon from Ilusha, handed it himself to mamma with a polite bow. She was so touched she burst into tears.
"Ilusha, darling, he's the one who loves his mamma!" she said tenderly, and immediately began wheeling the cannon back and forth on her lap again.
"Mamma, let me kiss your hand." The captain darted up to her at once and did so.
"And I've never seen such a charming fellow as this nice boy," said the grateful lady, pointing at Krassotkin.

"And I'll bring you as much powder as you like, Ilusha. We make our own powder now. Borovikov figured out how it's done — twenty-four parts saltpeter, ten of sulphur, and six of birchwood charcoal. It's all ground together, mixed into a paste with water, and rubbed through a fine sieve — that's how it's done."
"Smurov told me about your powder, only father says it's not real gunpowder," Ilusha said.
"Not real?" Kolya flushed. "It burns. I don't know, of course."
"No, I didn't mean that," the captain put in, looking guilty. "I only said real powder isn't made that way, but it doesn't matter — it can be made that way."

"I don't know, you'd know best. We lit some in a pomade jar, it burned beautifully, all burned away leaving just a tiny bit of ash. But that was only the paste, and if you rub it through ... well, you know best, I don't know.... And Bulkin's father thrashed him over our powder, did you hear?" he turned to Ilusha.
"Yes," Ilusha answered. He was listening to Kolya with intense interest and enjoyment.

"We'd made up a whole bottle of it and he kept it under his bed. His father found it. Said it might explode, and thrashed him on the spot. He was going to complain about me to the masters. He's not allowed to go around with me now — no one's allowed to go around with me now. Smurov isn't allowed to either — I've got a bad name with everyone. They say I'm a 'desperate character,'" Kolya smiled scornfully. "It all started with that business on the railway."

"Ah, we've heard about that exploit of yours, too," the captain cried. "How could you lie still on the track? Is it possible you weren't the least bit afraid, lying there under the train? Weren't you scared?"
The captain was abject in his flattery of Kolya.

"N—not especially," Kolya answered carelessly. "What's damaged my reputation around here more than anything was that cursed goose," he said, turning back to Ilusha. But though he kept up a careless air as he talked, he still couldn't help himself and kept losing the tone he was trying to hold.
"Ah! I heard about the goose!" Ilusha laughed, beaming all over. "They told me, but I didn't understand it. Did they really take you to court?"

"The most stupid, trivial business — they made a mountain out of a molehill, as they always do," Kolya began carelessly. "I was walking through the market square here one day, just as they'd driven in the geese. I stopped and looked at them. All at once a fellow — he's an errand boy at Plotnikov's now — looked at me and said, 'What are you looking at the geese for?' I looked at him; he was a stupid, moon-faced fellow of twenty. I'm always on the side of the peasantry, you know. I like talking to peasants.... We've fallen behind the peasants — that's an axiom. I believe you're laughing, Karamazov?"
"No, heaven forbid, I'm listening," said Alyosha, with such a good-natured air that the sensitive Kolya was reassured at once.

"My theory, Karamazov, is clear and simple," he hurried on, pleased with himself. "I believe in the common people and I'm always glad to give them their due, but I'm not for spoiling them — that's a _sine qua non_.... But I was telling you about the goose. So I turned to the fool and answered, 'I'm wondering what the goose is thinking about.' He looked at me quite blankly. 'And what is the goose thinking about?' he asked. 'You see that cart full of oats?' I said. 'The oats are spilling out of the sack, and the goose has stuck its neck right under the wheel to gobble them up — you see?' 'I see that well enough,' he said. 'Well,' I said, 'if that cart were to move on a little, would it break the goose's neck or not?' 'It'd break it for sure,' and he grinned all over his face, thoroughly delighted. 'Come on then,' I said, 'let's try it.' 'Let's,' he said. And it didn't take us long to arrange: he took hold of the bridle without being noticed, and I stood to one side to direct the goose. And the owner wasn't watching, he was talking to someone, so I had nothing to do — the goose stuck its head in after the oats on its own, under the cart, right under the wheel. I winked at the lad, he tugged the bridle, and crack. The goose's neck snapped clean in half. And, as luck would have it, all the peasants saw us right at that moment, and they raised a ruckus at once. 'You did that on purpose!' 'No, not on purpose.' 'Yes, you did, on purpose!' Well, they shouted, 'Take him to the justice of the peace!' They took me too. 'You were in on it too,' they said, 'you helped, everyone in the market knows you!' And, for some reason, I really am known all over the market," Kolya added, with some pride. "We all trooped off to the justice's, and they brought the goose along too. The fellow was crying, in a great panic, blubbering just like a woman. And the farmer kept shouting you could kill any number of geese that way. Well, of course, there were witnesses. The justice settled it in a minute: the farmer was to be paid a rouble for the goose, and the fellow got to keep the goose. And he was warned not to play tricks like that again. And the fellow kept blubbering like a woman. 'It wasn't me,' he said, 'he put me up to it,' and pointed at me. I answered, perfectly composed, that I hadn't put him up to anything, that I'd simply stated a general proposition, spoken hypothetically. The justice of the peace smiled, and then got annoyed at himself for smiling. 'I'll complain to your teachers about you, so that in future you won't waste your time on general propositions instead of sitting over your books and learning your lessons.' He never actually complained to the teachers — that was a joke — but the story got around and reached the teachers' ears anyway. They've got long ears, you know! The classical master, Kolbasnikov, was particularly scandalized by it, but Dardanelov got me off again. But Kolbasnikov's furious with everyone these days, like a green donkey. Did you know, Ilusha, he just got married, got a dowry of a thousand roubles, and his bride's an absolute fright, first-class, bottom of the barrel. The third-year fellows wrote an epigram about it:
Astounding news has reached the class, Kolbasnikov has been an ass.

And so on — it's awfully funny, I'll bring it to you later. I've got nothing against Dardanelov, he's a learned man, no doubt about that. I respect men like that, and it's not because he stood up for me."
"But you took him down over who founded Troy!" Smurov put in suddenly, plainly proud of Krassotkin at that moment. He'd especially loved the story of the goose.
"Did you really take him down?" the captain asked, in a flattering tone. "On the question of who founded Troy? We heard about it — Ilusha told me at the time."
"He knows everything, father, he knows more than any of us!" Ilusha put in. "He just pretends to be ordinary, but really he's top of the class in every subject...."
Ilusha looked at Kolya with boundless happiness.

"Oh, that's all nonsense about Troy, a trivial matter. I consider it an unimportant question," Kolya said, with haughty humility. He'd fully recovered his dignity by now, though he was still a little uneasy. He sensed he'd gotten quite worked up, and had talked about the goose, for instance, with too little restraint, while Alyosha had looked serious and hadn't said a word the whole time. And the vain boy was gradually starting to be gnawed by a fear that Alyosha's silence meant he despised him, thought he was showing off in front of him. If Alyosha dared think anything like that, Kolya would—
"I consider the question a perfectly trivial one," he said again, sharply, with pride.

"And I know who founded Troy," said a boy who hadn't spoken until then, to everyone's surprise. He'd been silent, apparently shy. He was a pretty boy of about eleven, named Kartashov. He sat near the door. Kolya looked at him with dignified astonishment.

The fact was, the identity of the founders of Troy had become a secret across the whole school, a secret that could only be uncovered by reading Smaragdov, and nobody had a copy of Smaragdov but Kolya. One day, while Kolya's back was turned, Kartashov had hastily opened Smaragdov, which lay among Kolya's books, and immediately hit upon the passage about the founding of Troy. This had happened quite a while before, but he'd felt uneasy and couldn't bring himself to announce publicly that he too knew who'd founded Troy, afraid of what might happen and of Krassotkin somehow shaming him over it. But now he couldn't resist saying it. He'd been longing to for weeks.

"Well, who did found it?" Kolya asked, turning to him with haughty condescension. He could see from his face that he really did know, and instantly decided how to handle it. There was, so to speak, a false note in the general harmony.

"Troy was founded by Teucer, Dardanus, Ilius, and Tros," the boy rattled off at once, and in the same instant blushed, blushed so hard it was painful to look at him. But the other boys stared at him — stared at him for a full minute — and then every eye swung at once toward Kolya, who was still studying the audacious boy with disdainful composure.
"In what sense did they found it?" he condescended to say at last. "And what exactly is meant by founding a city or a state? What did they do — do you suppose they each went and laid a brick?"
There was laughter. The offending boy went from pink to crimson. He said nothing, on the verge of tears. Kolya held him in suspense a minute longer.

"Before you talk about a historical event like the founding of a nation, you first need to understand what you even mean by it," he admonished him, in stern, incisive tones. "But I attach no importance to these old wives' tales, and I don't think much of world history in general," he added carelessly, addressing the whole room.
"World history?" the captain asked, looking almost frightened.

"Yes, world history! It's the study of humanity's successive follies, and nothing more. The only subjects I respect are mathematics and natural science," said Kolya. He was showing off, and he glanced at Alyosha; his was the only opinion he feared here. But Alyosha was still silent, still just as serious. If Alyosha had said one word, it would have stopped him — but Alyosha was silent, and "it might be the silence of contempt," which finally irritated Kolya.
"The classical languages too ... they're simply madness, nothing more. You seem to disagree with me again, Karamazov?"
"I don't agree," said Alyosha, with a faint smile.

"The study of the classics, if you want my opinion, is nothing but a police measure — that's the real reason it was introduced into our schools." Kolya was starting to run out of breath again. "Latin and Greek were brought in because they're deadly dull and they stupefy the mind. It was dull enough before, so what could they do to make things duller? It was senseless enough already, so what could they do to make it more senseless? So they came up with Greek and Latin. That's my opinion, and I hope I never change it," Kolya finished abruptly. His cheeks were flushed.
"That's true," Smurov agreed suddenly, in a ringing tone of conviction. He'd been listening carefully.
"And yet he's top of the class in Latin himself!" one of the boys cried out suddenly.
"Yes, father, he says that and he's still top in Latin," Ilusha echoed.

"What of it?" Kolya thought it necessary to defend himself, though the praise was very sweet to him. "I'm slogging away at Latin because I have to, because I promised my mother I'd pass my exams, and I think that whatever you do, it's worth doing well. But deep down I have a profound contempt for the classics and the whole fraud of it.... Don't you agree, Karamazov?"
"Why 'fraud'?" Alyosha smiled again.

"Well, all the classical authors have been translated into every language, so it wasn't for the sake of studying the classics that they brought in Latin, but purely as a police measure, to stupefy the mind. So what else can you call it but a fraud?"
"But who taught you all this?" Alyosha cried, genuinely surprised at last.

"First of all, I'm perfectly capable of thinking for myself, without being taught. Besides, what I just said about the classics being translated — our teacher Kolbasnikov said that to the whole of the third class."
"The doctor's here!" cried Nina, who'd been silent until then.

A carriage belonging to Madame Hohlakov pulled up at the gate. The captain, who'd been expecting the doctor all morning, dashed headlong out to meet him. "Mamma" pulled herself together and put on a dignified air. Alyosha went over to Ilusha and began straightening his pillows. Nina, from her invalid chair, watched anxiously as he tidied the bed. The boys hurriedly said their goodbyes. A few of them promised to come back that evening. Kolya called Perezvon and the dog jumped off the bed.
"I'm not leaving, I'm not leaving," Kolya said quickly to Ilusha. "I'll wait in the hallway and come back once the doctor's gone — I'll come back with Perezvon."

But by now the doctor had entered — an important-looking man with long dark whiskers and a shiny, clean-shaven chin, wearing a bearskin coat. As he crossed the threshold he stopped short, taken aback; he probably thought he'd come to the wrong place. "What's this? Where am I?" he muttered, not removing his coat or his peaked sealskin cap. The crowd, the poverty of the room, the washing hanging on a line in the corner, all threw him off. The captain, bent double, bowed low before him.
"It's here, sir, right here, sir," he muttered obsequiously; "it's here, you've come to the right place, you were on your way to us..."
"Sne-gi-ryov?" the doctor said loudly and pompously. "Mr. Snegiryov — is that you?"
"That's me, sir!"
"Ah!"

The doctor cast another squeamish glance around the room and threw off his coat, revealing the impressive decoration at his neck. The captain caught the fur coat in midair, and the doctor took off his cap.
"Where's the patient?" he asked, with emphasis.
